parsed_answer.content: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is the paradigm that shifts focus from procedural logic—sequences of operations—to the modeling of real-world entities through objects. In Java, this is enforced by the JVM's class-loading mechanism, where every object is an instance of a class residing in the heap. Encapsulation is the practice of bundling data (fields) and methods that operate on that data within a single unit, restricting direct access via access modifiers like private to maintain internal state integrity. Abstraction simplifies complex reality by modeling classes based on essential characteristics, often using abstract classes or interfaces to hide implementation details from the consumer. Inheritance allows a class to derive properties and behaviors from a parent, promoting code reuse and establishing an 'is-a' relationship, though it must be used judiciously to avoid fragile base class problems. Polymorphism, specifically subtype polymorphism, enables objects to be treated as instances of their parent class, allowing the JVM to invoke the correct overridden method at runtime via dynamic method dispatch (vtable lookup).

items: Encapsulation is enforced by the Java compiler; private fields prevent external classes from corrupting the internal state, forcing interaction through public getters/setters or business methods.
Abstraction is implemented through interfaces, which define a contract (a set of method signatures) without dictating how the logic is performed, allowing for interchangeable implementations.
Inheritance creates a tight coupling between classes. In modern Java design, favor composition over inheritance to avoid deep, rigid class hierarchies that are difficult to refactor.

Polymorphism relies on the JVM's dynamic method dispatch. When you call a method on an object reference, the JVM looks at the actual object type in the heap, not the reference type, to determine which implementation to execute.

parsed_answer.content: A common trap for junior developers is 'Inheritance Abuse.' Just because Class B has a method that Class A needs, it doesn't mean B should extend A. If you find yourself overriding methods just to throw UnsupportedOperationException, your inheritance hierarchy is likely broken. Always prefer composition (injecting an object into another) to keep your code modular and testable.
